method: Work backward one generation at a time from a living person. Each step must be anchored by a record that names the person, not a story about them. Story stays in the Family Story Archive as SOURCE STORY; the record goes in EVIDENCE.

sources.title: 1950 → 1900 US federal census
sources.covers: Every household by name; 1900 gives birth month and year; 1910 and 1930 often give years married; 1950 released April 2022
sources.why: Fastest way to walk back 3–4 generations in one sitting.

sources.title: Social Security SS-5 applications and Claims Index
sources.covers: Applicant's parents' names, including the mother's maiden name
where: SSA FOIA request for the original SS-5
sources.cost: index free–paid; SS-5 copy has a fee
sources.why: Often the first record that names a great-grandmother's maiden name.

sources.title: State death certificates and WWI/WWII draft cards
sources.covers: Parents' names, birthplace, informant; draft cards give exact birth date and town
sources.why: The informant line often names who knew the family story.

sources.title: 1880 and 1870 US federal census
sources.covers: 1870 is the first census that names every Black American; 1880 adds relationship to head of household
sources.why: 1870 is the brick wall. Everything earlier needs the records below.

sources.title: 1890 population schedules
sources.covers: About 99% destroyed in the 1921 Commerce Building fire in Washington, DC; surviving fragments plus the 1890 Union veterans and widows schedule
sources.why: Explains why a family vanishes between 1880 and 1900. Not a dead end, just a gap.

sources.title: Freedman's Savings and Trust Company (Freedman's Bank) registers, 1865–1874
sources.covers: Depositors with parents, siblings, children, spouse, former enslaver and plantation
sources.why: One card can name three generations at once.

sources.title: Freedmen's Bureau records, 1865–1872
sources.covers: Labor contracts, marriages, rations, schools, complaints
where: Discovering the Freedmen's Bureau / Smithsonian transcriptions
sources.why: Names people right at emancipation, often with the former enslaver.

sources.title: 1850 and 1860 slave schedules
sources.covers: Enslaved people listed by age, sex and color under the enslaver's name; not by their own name
sources.why: Used only after the enslaver is identified from SRC-006/007; match ages, never assume.

sources.title: Extra Census Bulletin: The Five Civilized Tribes in Indian Territory — the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek and Seminole Nations
sources.covers: 1890 census narrative and statistics for Indian Territory, including Freedmen and intermarried citizens; Census Office, Department of the Interior; Robert P. Porter, Superintendent; Thomas Donaldson, expert special agent
sources.why: The document from the researcher's video. It is CONTEXT, not a name roll: it shows who lived where and how they were counted. Names are in SRC-010 to SRC-013.

sources.title: Dawes Rolls — Final Rolls of Citizens and Freedmen of the Five Civilized Tribes, 1898–1914
sources.covers: Enrollment cards with parents, ages, blood quantum (by blood) or Freedman status, plus full application jackets
sources.why: The single most important roll for Black families with Indian Territory roots. Freedmen cards are a separate series — search both.

sources.title: Wallace Roll (1890) and Kern-Clifton Roll (1896–97) of Cherokee Freedmen
sources.covers: Cherokee Freedmen by name before Dawes
sources.why: Puts a family in the Cherokee Nation a decade before Dawes.

sources.title: Guion Miller Roll and applications, 1906–1910 (Eastern Cherokee claims)
sources.covers: About 46,000 applications; many from Black families claiming Cherokee descent; each has a written family history and a decision
sources.why: Even a REJECTED application is gold: it preserves the family's own words from 1907 and names relatives.

sources.title: Indian Census Rolls, 1885–1940
sources.covers: Annual rolls by agency, including the Blackfeet Agency in Montana
sources.why: The direct test of a Blackfeet (Montana) connection: if the line was enrolled Blackfeet, they appear here year after year.

sources.title: Historic newspapers and 'Information Wanted' ads
sources.covers: Formerly enslaved people searching for family by name, place and enslaver
where: Last Seen: Finding Family After Slavery (Villanova)
sources.why: Family members describing each other in their own words.

sources.title: DNA — autosomal test plus matching
sources.covers: Living cousins and the shared ancestors they have already documented
sources.why: Best use is CONNECTING to cousins with trees. Ethnicity percentages can't prove or rule out a specific tribe.

intake_required_from_chairman: Full names, approximate birth years and states or counties for parents, grandparents and great-grandparents (as far as known)
Which family line carries the Blackfoot / Blackfeet story, and the exact words the elders used
What the sister found and which site she used (FamilySearch, Ancestry, a DNA test), so the team starts where she stopped
Any family Bible pages, obituaries, funeral programs or photos with names written on them
